brief: US-Iran strikes pushed oil and long yields higher (30y above 5%, real yields near 3%), pressuring mortgages, capex, AI financing and equity valuations, but the crude response has been contained: Kpler estimates non-Iranian Gulf exports recovered to about 9mb/d, 65% of pre-war levels, as dark transits and bypass routes weaken the link between visible Hormuz traffic and market barrels. Weaker Chinese demand and Trump's midterm sensitivity cap crude, but refined-product supply stays constrained, so diesel, jet fuel and gasoline still transmit the shock. The author argues repeated supply shocks are now a structural feature of a fragmented economy, so the Fed can no longer look through them as it could when inflation was low and anchored. Waller wants to hold if August CPI stays benign, believing inflation is better than core PCE shows; Warsh disagrees, arguing the summer's prints don't prove real progress, and his own standard for holding points toward hiking given elevated inflation, near-maximum employment and growth above 2%. The author concludes a well-signaled September hike would not mechanically lower the 30y yield but could cut inflation uncertainty and term premium, more constructive for risk assets than a hold that leaves bonds to do the Fed's work.
